title: Further reflection
text: FURTHER REFLECTION SOME QUESTIONS TO THINK ABOUT… At the end of the novel Stevens has a conversation with a stranger on a bench who makes reference to the title by encouraging Stevens to enjoy the remainder of his day given that he has “done his day’s work” (p. 244). Why do you think Ishiguro includes this brief conversation at the close of the novel? Do you think Stevens is likely to heed the stranger’s advice? Could Ishiguro have set this novel in any time and place? What is the significance of the particular historical context in furthering the novel’s themes and message? To what extent do you agree that Stevens is a reliable narrative voice, and that we can trust his reporting of the events of the story? One of the themes that appears in many of Ishiguro’s works is the inevitability of human failure and shortcoming. Is this applicable to The Remains of the Day ? Why/why not? Due to the fact that Stevens’ professional standards and expectations are so high, he often makes comments that to us seem comically exaggerated, such as when he compares the butler’s pantry to “general’s headquarters during a battle” (p. 165). How is Stevens’ narration an effective way to insert humour into the novel? When Miss Kenton and Stevens finally meet at the end of the novel, Stevens remarks “Well, whatever awaits me, Mrs Benn, I know I’m not awaited by emptiness. If only I were. But oh no, there’s work, work and more work” (p. 237). Discuss how Ishiguro creates this contrast between what the reader sees as empty and Stevens sees as meaningful. If you were to ask Stevens what the meaning of life was, what might he respond given what we know about his character? Throughout the novel, Stevens reflects on the ‘greatness’ of England, claiming that the stoicism and composure of an English butler is simply unrivalled. In your opinion, is Ishiguro celebrating this supposed ‘greatness’ or criticising it? Explain your answer. In 1928 all women and men over the age of 21 were granted the right to vote, resulting in universal suffrage. How does the question of the ordinary citizen’s role in national affairs surface in Ishiguro’s text?
